526.title: A fatherly household
526.hook: from Sextus: kindness, dignity without show, and patience with the unlearned (Meditations 1.9)
526.howItsDone: Readers who take this entry to heart often practice answering beginners' questions without impatience, and keep learning something new themselves.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Apollonius, steady through pain, grief and long illness. Your line was the same in pain.

Someone at work asks the question everyone else learned years ago. Where's the shared drive? What does that acronym mean? A sigh is right there, ready to be given. Anyone who has been new somewhere has heard that sigh from the other side. Book one's ninth entry is about a teacher who never gave it: a philosopher with a famous family name, and a whole house with a certain feel to it.
screen: `WHERE'S THE SHARED DRIVE?` → `THE SIGH YOU COULD GIVE.` → `A FATHERLY HOUSEHOLD.`

segments.voice: First, Sextus. A philosopher from Chaeronea in Greece, and, ancient writers say, a relative of the writer Plutarch, perhaps his nephew. Marcus studied with him. Second, the household. From Sextus, Marcus says, he learned kindness, and saw the example of a family governed in a fatherly way. Living by nature. Dignity without putting it on. Watching out for his friends' interests. Company so easy that it was more pleasant than any flattery, while everyone still respected him. Sextus was free of anger, Marcus says, and yet full of affection. Calm didn't make him cold. Third, the patience. Marcus learned from him to put up with people who don't know things, and with people who form opinions without thinking them through. Not to sneer, not to sigh, just to bear with them. At home, that's the parent who explains again. In school, it's the teacher who hears the same question for the twentieth time and answers it like the first. Fourth, the emperor goes to school. A later writer, Philostratus, tells a story that even as emperor, Marcus kept going to hear Sextus lecture. Asked where he was going, Marcus answered, roughly, that it's good even for an older man to learn, and he was off to Sextus to learn what he didn't yet know. Whether every word is accurate or not, it fits. It's easier to be patient with beginners when you never stop being one.

527.title: Correct without shaming
527.hook: from Alexander the grammarian: correct people's mistakes by saying the right thing yourself (Meditations 1.10)
527.howItsDone: Many parents, teachers and colleagues practice something like Alexander's way: they repeat the correct word or fact naturally in their reply instead of pointing out the mistake.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Sextus and his fatherly household. Your line was patient with the unlearned.

A four-year-old announces, I goed to the park. You have choices. You can say, no, it's went, say it again. Or you can say, you went to the park? What did you see? Most parents learn, sooner or later, that the second way works better, and nobody cries. Nearly two thousand years ago, a teacher of Greek grammar did the same with grown men, including a future emperor, and Marcus thought it worth a whole entry.
screen: `I GOED TO THE PARK.` → `YOU WENT? WHAT DID YOU SEE?` → `CORRECT WITHOUT SHAMING.`

segments.voice: First, the teacher. Alexander was a grammarian, a professional teacher of Greek language and literature, a respected job in Rome, and he taught the young Marcus. A grammarian's whole life is noticing mistakes. Second, what he didn't do. Marcus says he learned from Alexander not to find fault, and not to jump on people who used a clumsy word, a wrong form or an odd-sounding phrase. No pouncing. No public correction. Third, what he did instead. He would slip the right expression into the conversation himself, neatly: as part of his answer, or while agreeing with the person, or while talking with them about the real subject, the thing itself, not the word. The other person heard the right form, and nobody had been made small. Fourth, why it works. Corrected in front of others, people usually hear one thing: that they were wrong in public. The lesson vanishes under the embarrassment. Said right, in passing, the lesson arrives without the sting, and they can pick it up, or not. And notice Alexander's priority: the conversation stays on the subject, not the slip. This reaches past grammar. A friend mispronounces a name. A colleague gets a fact slightly wrong in a meeting. A parent uses an old word for something. Often the kindest correction is just the right word, said gently, in the next sentence. Marcus, who would one day have the power to humiliate anyone, wrote down a teacher who refused to.

528.title: Free speech and equal rights
528.hook: from Severus: the idea of a state with equal law and free speech (Meditations 1.14)
528.howItsDone: Readers who take this entry seriously often practice letting people they disagree with finish speaking, and say their own disagreements openly rather than hiding them.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Alexander, the grammarian who never pounced on a mistake. Your line was say it right, gently.

Here's a sentence from an unlikely pen. A man with an army, the final say in law, and the power of life and death over an empire writes in his private notebook that he's grateful someone taught him the idea of a state where the same law applies to everyone, where people have an equal right to speak, and where the ruler respects, above all, the freedom of the ruled.
screen: `AN EMPEROR'S PRIVATE NOTEBOOK.` → `THE SAME LAW FOR EVERYONE.` → `FREE SPEECH AND EQUAL RIGHTS.`

segments.voice: First, Severus. Marcus calls him my brother. He's probably Claudius Severus, a philosopher whose son married one of Marcus's daughters, so brother may be a family word, not a literal one. From him, Marcus says, he learned to love his family, truth and justice. Second, the heroes. Through Severus, Marcus came to know about Cato and Brutus, from the last days of the Roman Republic, and Thrasea and Helvidius, senators who stood up to emperors and were killed or exiled for it. An heir to the throne, learning to admire people who defied the throne. Third, the idea. From Severus, Marcus says, he received the idea of a state with one law for all, run on equal rights and equal freedom of speech, and of a monarchy that respects most of all the freedom of the governed. The same entry adds that Severus said plainly what he disapproved of, so his friends never had to guess. Fourth, honesty about Rome. Marcus's empire was not that state. Rome held slaves, and its law did not treat the powerful and the poor alike. Historians still argue about how far Marcus lived up to the idea. But the entry shows a ruler who kept, in his private notes, a picture of something better than the system he ran, and named the man who gave it to him. Equal voices start small. Not in a senate. At a table, when someone you disagree with is speaking, and you let them finish.

529.title: Maximus' good cheer
529.hook: from Maximus: self-command, cheerfulness in illness, doing duties without complaint (Meditations 1.15)
529.howItsDone: Some readers of the Meditations take Maximus as a model for doing tedious or hard tasks steadily and without complaint, especially when tired or unwell.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Severus, and the idea of one law and equal speech. Your line was equal voices.

Some people can't empty the dishwasher without a soundtrack of sighs. Others just do it. And now and then you meet someone who does the dull job, the hard job, even the job they're too sick for, and somehow makes the room lighter while they do it. What lingers is less what they said than the air around them. Marcus had a friend like that, a senator and Stoic named Claudius Maximus, and gave him a long, detailed portrait in book one.
screen: `A SOUNDTRACK OF SIGHS.` → `THE ONE WHO MAKES THE ROOM LIGHTER.` → `MAXIMUS' GOOD CHEER.`

segments.voice: First, who he was. Claudius Maximus was a Roman senator and a Stoic. He governed the province of Africa, and history happens to remember him as the judge at a famous trial there, where the writer Apuleius was accused of using magic to win a rich wife. Apuleius's speech in his own defense still survives. Second, the portrait. From Maximus, Marcus says, he learned to govern himself and not be pushed off course by anything. To be cheerful in every circumstance, illnesses included. To mix gentleness and dignity in the right measure. And to do the work in front of him without complaining. Third, the details. Everyone believed Maximus meant what he said, and that whatever he did, he did without bad intent. He never seemed astonished or rattled, never rushed, never put things off, never lost heart, and never laughed to cover up irritation. He was quick to do good and quick to forgive. And a lovely line: nobody ever felt looked down on by Maximus, and nobody ever dared think himself better than him. Fourth, cheer without complaint. The two sit together. Complaint is often the sound of carrying something while making sure everyone knows how heavy it is. Maximus carried it and kept the weight to himself, so the people around him could breathe easier. Later in the notebook, Marcus writes simply that Maximus died. Book one keeps him as Marcus saw him: doing the job in front of him, cheerfully, without a word about how hard it was.

530.title: Among the Quadi
530.hook: a note says book two was written in camp on the river Granua, at war
530.howItsDone: Some people who keep a journal in Marcus's spirit write wherever they happen to be, on commutes, breaks or travels, rather than waiting for a quiet desk.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Claudius Maximus, cheerful even when ill. Your line was no complaint.

Where do you picture the Meditations being written? A marble study, maybe, with a view over Rome. A quiet library. Scrolls, oil lamps, silence. Then you reach the end of book one, and there, in the manuscripts, is a short line that changes the picture. It isn't philosophy. It's a place name. Among the Quadi, at the Granua. A tribe and a river, far from Rome, on the edge of the empire, in the middle of a war.
screen: `A MARBLE STUDY IN ROME?` → `A LINE AT THE END OF BOOK ONE.` → `AMONG THE QUADI.`

segments.voice: First, the note. Between books one and two, the manuscripts carry a few words: among the Quadi, at the Granua. The Quadi were a Germanic people living north of the Danube. The Granua is a river there, usually identified with the Hron, which flows through what's now Slovakia. Second, the war. The historian Cassius Dio tells of Marcus on the Danube frontier, leading campaigns against the Marcomanni, the Quadi and other peoples, year after year. The emperor spent long seasons in army camps, in the cold, far from Rome. Third, where the note belongs. Scholars aren't agreed. It could close book one, or head book two. Some editors read it as a heading for book two, because a similar note, at Carnuntum, a legionary fortress on the Danube, stands before book three. Either way, at least some of this notebook was written in a camp, at war. Fourth, what that changes. Read book one again with a tent around it. A tired man at the frontier, far from his family, sat down and listed, one by one, the people who had made him who he was. A great-grandfather. A tutor. Rusticus. Apollonius. Sextus. Alexander. Severus. Maximus. Not a victory list. A gratitude list. And when book two begins tomorrow, the camp is still there.

531.title: Flesh, breath, ruling part
531.hook: you're flesh, breath and a ruling mind; don't let the mind be a slave (Meditations 2.2)
531.tomorrow: Throw away the thirst for books
531.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism do Marcus's three-part check (body, breath, mind) during the day, asking whether their mind is choosing or being pulled.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Quadi, the note that puts the notebook in an army camp. Your line was written in camp.

Book one was thanks. Book two, perhaps begun in camp, opens differently. After a first entry about the difficult people he'll meet today, read on this path before, Marcus turns to himself and does something like a doctor's exam. He takes himself apart into three pieces, names each one, and asks which of them is in charge. The first is the plainest: flesh.
screen: `BOOK TWO, PERHAPS IN CAMP.` → `A DOCTOR'S EXAM ON HIMSELF.` → `FLESH.`

segments.voice: First, the sentence. Section two opens, in Long's translation: "Whatever this is that I am, it is a little flesh and breath, and the ruling part." Notice the humility of whatever this is. The emperor of Rome isn't sure what he is, and he's starting from the ground up. Second, flesh. He's blunt here: as if you were already dying, he tells himself, look down on the flesh. Then he looks at it like an anatomy student: blood, bones, a woven net of nerves, veins and arteries. He doesn't call the body evil. He's refusing to let it be the thing that runs his life. Third, breath. What is it? Air, and not even the same air from one moment to the next, breathed out and drawn in, again and again. You've been watching it on this path for hundreds of days; Marcus noticed it too, perhaps in a tent. Fourth, the ruling part, the mind that judges and chooses. The Stoics called it the hegemonikon, the part that leads. And here Marcus gives himself an order. You're no longer young, he says. Don't let this part be a slave any longer, pulled by strings like a puppet, jerked into selfish moves. Don't let it grumble at the present or shrink from the future. That's the picture to carry. The flesh pulls. The appetites pull. Other people's opinions pull. Everyone has strings. The question is whether the ruling part is holding them, or hanging from them.
screen: `A LITTLE FLESH, BREATH, RULING PART.` · `FLESH: BLOOD, BONE, A NET.` · `BREATH: AIR, NEVER THE SAME.` · `THE RULING PART HOLDS THE STRINGS.` · then, large: `NOT A PUPPET.`

Flesh. The first of Marcus's three parts: a little flesh, breath, and the ruling mind, which shouldn't be pulled by strings like a puppet. Today's word.

532.title: Throw away the thirst for books
532.word: Throw away the thirst for books
532.hook: stop craving more books, and die content, not grumbling (Meditations 2.3)
532.howItsDone: Some readers of Marcus limit how much new reading they take on and spend more time rereading and practicing a few texts they trust.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was flesh, the first of three: flesh, breath and the ruling part. Your line was not a puppet. This week brought Marcus's debts to a gentle Sextus, a tactful grammarian, a Severus he called brother, who loved free speech, and a cheerful Maximus, then the camp.

The pile by the bed. The library holds. The audiobooks at one and a half speed. The saved articles you'll get to someday. For a lot of curious people, the next book is a kind of hunger that never quite ends. Now, in the third entry of book two, Marcus says something odd for a man who loved reading.
screen: `THE PILE BY THE BED.` → `THE NEXT BOOK, ALWAYS.` → `THROW AWAY THE THIRST FOR BOOKS.`

segments.voice: First, what comes before it. Section three is a quick sketch of how Marcus sees the world: everything from the gods is full of providence, everything hangs together, and what serves the whole is good for each part. Let these be enough for you, he tells himself; hold them as settled. Second, the line. And throw away the thirst for books, he says, so that you don't die grumbling, but cheerful, truthful, and thankful to the gods from the heart. Third, the word thirst. He doesn't say throw away books. This is a man who thanked Rusticus for lending him Epictetus and thanked his great-grandfather for good teachers. The problem isn't reading. It's thirst: the feeling that the answer is always in the next book, so you never have to live by the ones you've read. Seneca said the same in his second letter, read on this path this year: a mind that's everywhere is nowhere. Fourth, why it matters at the end. Marcus ties this to dying content. Picture someone at the end of life still anxious about all the books they never got to. Now picture someone who read a few, lived by them, and could say thank you. That second ending is the one he wants. There's a gentle joke in today, too: a daily path built on reading, telling you to put a book down. But that's the point of a daily path. One small thing, practiced, instead of a hundred things collected.
screen: `LET THESE BE ENOUGH FOR YOU.` · `DON'T DIE GRUMBLING.` · `NOT BOOKS, BUT THE THIRST.` · `READ A FEW; LIVE BY THEM.` · then, large: `ENOUGH READING.`

segments.voice: Picture your own pile, the books, the podcasts, the saved articles, and feel the small tug of it. Now pick one thing you've already read or heard that's genuinely worth living by, a line, a story, a rule, and hold it. If it were enough for today, what would you do with it?
Throw away the thirst for books. Not the books, the thirst, so that you live by what you've read and end your days thankful, not grumbling. Today's word.
screen: `THROW AWAY THE THIRST FOR BOOKS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: enough reading. Enough isn't none; it's enough to live on. Day five hundred thirty-two, the end of a week.

chat.who: a friend with a huge reading list
chat.says: Did Marcus Aurelius really tell people to stop reading books?
options: No, just the thirst: chasing the next book instead of living what you've read.
Yes, he decided books were a distraction and gave up reading for good.
No, he meant read faster, so you can finish more books before you die.
chat.meaning: In 2.3 Marcus throws away the thirst for books, not the books, so he can die cheerful and thankful, not grumbling.
